hypotheses.name: Lexical recycling
hypotheses.claim: Human passages reuse the identical content word instead of reaching for a synonym, giving a markedly lower type-token ratio (content-word TTR 0.66 / 0.71 / 0.73 for the three human exemplars vs. seed mean 0.80, range 0.72-0.88) and more verbatim repeated 4-grams (1 / 6 / 3 vs. seed mean 1.3). Miedema says 'committees' eight times and 'come together' three times in 346 words; Champagne runs 'build a stronger, more resilient Canada' four times almost unchanged. The AI-drafted seeds vary the wording on each pass. If this is wrong, human legislative prose should show synonym rotation at the same rate as the seeds.
hypotheses.how: Choose two or three key nouns and one slogan phrase. Repeat the exact same word 6-9 times per 350 words and let one 4-or-more-word phrase recur verbatim 2-3 times. Never substitute a synonym for a term you have already used; if you catch yourself writing 'the ecosystem' for 'the broadcasting system', revert to the original word.

hypotheses.name: No one-beat sentence
hypotheses.claim: Humans almost never isolate a short sentence for percussive emphasis, and they run longer sentences than the AI drafts. Sentences of six words or fewer: 0 / 1 / 1 in the human exemplars vs. a seed mean of 2.8 (up to 6). Sentences of nine words or fewer: 1 / 4 / 2 vs. seed mean 5.6. Conversely humans carry more 35+ word sentences (2 / 3 / 2 vs. seed mean 1.2) and higher maxima (57 / 49 / 42 words vs. seed mean 41). Seed punch lines like 'Naming femicide matters.' or 'Fuel costs drive the cost of living.' have no human counterpart here.
hypotheses.how: Allow at most one sentence under ten words per 350 words, and none under seven. Include at least two sentences over 40 words. Where you would normally break out a three-word emphatic beat, splice it onto the preceding sentence with a comma or 'and'.

hypotheses.name: Tail after the payload
hypotheses.claim: Human sentences put their strongest element in the middle and then keep going, adding participial or prepositional tails, so emphasis never lands at the end. Seeds obey end-focus. Human instances: 'Committees produce extensive and comprehensive reports, thereby adding to greater transparency for Canadians by ensuring public access to information about the government's work'; 'By taking part directly in our shared successes by investing in the fund, Canadians will be given the opportunity to share in our growth and contribute to the country we are building together.' Count of 'by + -ing': 2 / 2 / 0 in humans vs. a seed mean of 0.31, and humans stack the same preposition twice in one sentence, which a drafter would deduplicate.
hypotheses.how: After the strongest word in a sentence, append one more clause introduced by 'by -ing', 'thereby -ing', 'so that', or 'while'. Do not deduplicate a preposition that then appears twice ('by taking part... by investing'). End the sentence on the least interesting phrase it contains.

hypotheses.name: Additive, not the negated-foil reframe
hypotheses.claim: Seeds define things by knocking down a foil and flipping ('Violence against women is not abstract. It is not rare. It is not confined to headlines'; 'That is not just a number. It is tangible, meaningful relief'). Humans assert positively and then add another positive assertion. Negation reframes (a negated clause followed immediately by an 'It/This/That is' correction): 0 / 0 / 1 in humans vs. seed mean 1.4; sentence-initial 'It/This/That is not': 0 / 0 / 1 vs. 0.75; 'not just / not only / not merely': 0 / 0 / 2 vs. 0.5.
hypotheses.how: Budget at most one 'X is not Y, it is Z' construction per 350 words. Everywhere else, state the claim positively and follow it with a second positive claim on the same subject rather than with a contrast. Delete every 'not just a ___, but a ___' you write.

hypotheses.name: Lists overrun and decay
hypotheses.claim: Human enumerations continue past their rhetorically optimal stopping point and finish on the weakest member; seed enumerations close on the strongest. MacKinnon runs 'would remain intact' three times, then keeps going into 'Ministers would continue to testify at committee' and finally 'Government officials would continue to testify before those same committees' - a near-duplicate at lower stakes. Miedema's list 'from business leaders to academics, scientists and Canadians from across this great country' has an unclosed pair in the middle and dissolves into a relative clause. Seeds close cleanly: 'rise early, work long hours, drive trucks, build the homes, harvest the crops and keep this country moving.'
hypotheses.how: Write the list, identify its climactic item, then add one or two further items after it, each of lower stakes than the last, with the final item a near-restatement of the one before it in slightly different grammar. Do not prune the redundant item.

hypotheses.name: Anticlimactic ending
hypotheses.claim: The human passage ends on procedural low-wattage restatement, not a button. Endings observed: 'Through this process, we learn about what worked well, what did not and how to avoid challenges that other countries have experienced'; 'Government officials would continue to testify before those same committees'; a passive coil ('Canadians will be given the opportunity to share in our growth and contribute to the country we are building together'). Every high-scoring seed ends on an epigram or a scored point: 'While the Liberals broke it, Conservatives will fix it'; 'Fuel costs drive the cost of living'; 'Hate crimes and gender-based crimes will face the full extent of the law.'
hypotheses.how: Write the punchy closing line, then delete it. End instead on a sentence that restates the previous sentence with a smaller subject, or on a trailing subordinate clause ('...that other countries have experienced'). Never let the final sentence be the shortest or the most quotable in the passage.

hypotheses.name: Abstract subject, long cold open
hypotheses.claim: Human sentences frequently take an abstract process noun as grammatical subject with a light verb ('Participation in committees gives members the opportunity to...', 'Robust and constructive debate in committees is the means through which...', 'This engagement of experts, stakeholders and citizens acts as a bridge', 'An important aspect of committees is that they provide a mechanism for members to cultivate...'), and the passage opens cold with a long sentence: mean length of the first three sentences is 23.8 words for humans vs. 17.5 for seeds. Seeds open on a concrete agent or a short hook ('The truckers delivering groceries pay more for fuel'; 'Let me begin with the middle-class tax cut'; 'Safety cannot begin only after harm has occurred').
hypotheses.how: For roughly one sentence in four, make the subject an abstract noun phrase (Participation in / Engagement of / The discussions and insights that X generate) and the verb a light one (gives, provides, acts as, is the means through which). Open the passage with a 20+ word sentence that carries no hook and assumes the reader is already mid-argument.

hypotheses.name: Unglossed institutional idiom plus an unreturned aside
hypotheses.claim: Humans name procedural objects without explaining them and drop asides that go nowhere; seeds attach an explanatory appositive to every named object and stay on the argument. Human unglossed terms: 'the main estimates tabled this year', 'associate members or substitutes', 'our comportment', 'consistent with long-standing practices of the House and other Westminster parliaments'. Human asides: 'I see that my colleagues are smiling. I understand why, because...' (reacts to the room, abandoned immediately); 'I will now go back to the practical effects on committees' (admits a digression the reader never saw). Room-deixis count 1 / 3 / 2 in humans vs. seed mean 0.44. Seeds gloss: 'now carry the burden of demonstrating a reverse onus, in particular demonstrating why they should be released on bail'; 'Bill C-10, the commissioner for modern treaty implementation act. The bill would create a new officer of Parliament supported by a new federal office, with a mandate to...'
hypotheses.how: Use one or two procedural terms with no apposition and no definition, as if the audience already knows them. Then insert one sentence that reacts to something happening in the room, or that announces a return from a detour, and do not develop it or refer to it again.

hypotheses.name: Downgraded modality on your own proposal
hypotheses.claim: Humans attach minimizers to their strongest claims and connect with flat additives, where seeds escalate. Human instances: 'relationships that may be a little less partisan', 'important, if not paramount', 'a reasonable proposal', 'Committee work can also bring international perspectives', 'can help facilitate'. Hedge counts 2 / 0 / 6 vs. seed mean 1.4; 'also' 1.0 vs. 0.62; flat connectives 'Further / Moreover / In addition' 0.67 vs. 0.06. This is the least robust of the nine: Champagne (human, 45) has zero hedges and five superlatives, and the human sample is only three segments, all Liberal front-bench procedural speech, while the seeds skew toward opposition attack rhetoric - so party and genre are partly confounded with class throughout.
hypotheses.how: Take the passage's strongest claim about your own side's proposal and downgrade it with 'may', 'a little', 'if not', 'can also', or the adjective 'reasonable'. Join paragraphs with 'Further,' or 'also' rather than with a contrast or a rhetorical pivot, and avoid superlatives applied to your own measure ('bold', 'transformative', 'most significant in generations').
